passage: Pema's "I'm fine" was the third one I'd heard that morning, and I sit right next to her, so I noticed. Her eyes looked heavy and she had barely touched her tiffin at recess. When Ms Rao asked who could stay after school to help with the stage, Pema said yes before anyone else, and she smiled quickly. I don't know why she said yes. Maybe she wanted to be useful, or feared saying no would look lazy. At the gate I said, "You seem really tired. Do you want to skip the staying and just go home? I can tell Ms Rao." She looked at me a bit surprised, then whispered, "Actually, yes." Ira.

qa.a: Ira had heard it three times.

qa.q: What might Pema have been feeling when she volunteered to stay?

qa.a: Ira named the tiredness without judgement, offered to tell the teacher and let Pema choose.

qa.q: How might Ms Rao see Pema's quick yes?
qa.a: She likely took it at face value, as a keen student, since Pema smiled and showed no sign of trouble.

Monday. At football practice Bhupen said "I'm fine" when Coach asked why he was so quiet. His friend Alka looked at his bag: he had skipped lunch again and his hands were unsteady on the ball.
Wednesday. Alka waited by the gate and said, "You've been carrying a lot. What do you need? Even one thing." Bhupen said, "I didn't want to be a bother. I just need to eat properly and sleep before the test."
Friday. Bhupen walked up to Coach himself: "I've been overwhelmed. Can I sit out half the practice today?" Coach said yes. Bhupen felt lighter afterwards, and he told Alka thanks.

qa.q: What did Bhupen say when the coach asked why he was quiet?
qa.a: He said, "I'm fine."

qa.q: Why did Bhupen not tell anyone how he was really feeling at first?
qa.a: He did not want to be a bother, which suggests he worried about seeming needy. He may also have been too tired to explain himself.

qa.q: What small step helped Bhupen on Friday?
qa.a: He plainly told Coach he was overwhelmed and asked to sit out half the practice, so the small problem did not grow.

qa.q: How might the coach see Bhupen's request?
qa.a: Coach may be relieved that Bhupen said it, and glad to understand why Bhupen had been quiet. 🙂

grounding: A teen hides needs to avoid burdening others, then learns to state them plainly.

passage:
Vaibhav, you keep saying "I'm fine, Mama" when you're clearly not. Sit, let me tell you about your Varun Mama at fifteen.
I was in a hostel in Dehradun. The mess closed at eight, and every Tuesday I had football till eight-thirty. So on Tuesdays I didn't eat dinner. For a whole term. I told nobody. I thought asking for food would make me look like a baby, or a burden on the warden.
When friends asked, I said, "I'm fine, I ate." I got thinner. I started dozing in first period.
Then the warden, Mr Pinto, noticed I'd stopped joking at night. He called me in and asked, just once, "When did you last eat properly?" I cried, like a fool, right there.
From the next Tuesday, the cook kept a plate for me. One plate. That's all it needed. One sentence from me, months earlier.

qa.q: When did the mess close?
qa.a: The mess closed at eight.

qa.q: Why did Varun tell everyone he was fine?
qa.a: He was afraid that asking for food would make him look needy, like a baby or a burden, so he hid his hunger even as he grew tired.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed things?
qa.a: The warden noticed Varun had gone quiet and asked when he last ate properly, and then a plate was kept for him every Tuesday.

qa.q: How might Mr Pinto have seen Varun's change at night?
qa.a: Mr Pinto likely read the lost jokes as a sign that something was wrong, which is why he asked a direct, gentle question.

grounding: The elder's story shows a teen hiding hunger and tiredness behind "I'm fine" and an adult noticing withdrawal before it grew worse.

passage:
The school trip to the hills was supposed to end at four, but the bus broke down in the rain on a narrow ghat road. By six, forty students were squeezed into a roadside tea shack.
Jasleen sat in the corner with her jacket zipped to her chin. She had been soaked since noon and her throat hurt. When her friends offered chai, she smiled. "I'm fine, I'm not even cold."
Vishal Sir, counting heads for the fourth time, noticed she hadn't said a word in an hour. Usually she was the loudest.
He crouched beside her. "Jasleen, you've gone quiet. Honestly, how are you?"
She hesitated. "Cold. My throat hurts. I didn't want to make a fuss when the bus is already broken."
"This is exactly when to make a fuss." He gave her his dry fleece and a hot chai, and phoned her mother. "If you still feel unwell tomorrow, get it checked."

qa.q: How many students were squeezed into the roadside tea shack?
qa.a: Forty students were squeezed into the tea shack.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen say she was fine?
qa.a: She was cold and unwell but didn't want to be a burden when everyone was already stuck, so she hid her needs to avoid making a fuss.

qa.q: What did Vishal Sir notice, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He noticed she had gone quiet for an hour when she was usually loud, and asking gently brought out that she was cold and unwell.

qa.q: What would change if Jasleen had said what she needed earlier?
qa.a: She could have had the fleece and chai sooner, before the cold and sore throat got worse.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager saying "I'm fine" while unwell to avoid being a burden, and a teacher noticing withdrawal.

subtype: Hiding needs to avoid burdening others [Regulating]
passage:
Every afternoon that summer, Indu picked up her two younger brothers from school in Hyderabad, gave them lunch, helped with homework and kept them out of trouble until her parents got home at eight.
When her father, Lalit, asked, "All okay, beta?" she said, "Yes, fine." Every day.
But Lalit started noticing things. She had stopped humming in the kitchen. Her own books lay unopened on the table. One night she fell asleep sitting up.
On Sunday he made two cups of tea and sat beside her on the balcony. "Indu, you've gone quiet. I'm not angry. What's hard right now?"
She held the cup for a long moment. "Everything. I have no time for my own studies. I'm tired all the time. I didn't want to say, because you're both working so hard."
Lalit nodded slowly. "Thank you for saying it. Let's change the plan together."

qa.q: What time did Indu's parents get home?
qa.a: Her parents got home at eight.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling underneath her daily "Yes, fine"?
qa.a: Indu felt overwhelmed and exhausted, but afraid of adding to her parents' burden since they were working so hard.

qa.q: What small step did Lalit take that helped?
qa.a: He noticed her withdrawal, sat with her over tea, said he wasn't angry, and asked what was hard, which let her state her needs plainly.

qa.q: How might Indu's younger brothers see those afternoons?
qa.a: They probably saw only their big sister managing everything and had no idea how tired and stretched she felt.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager hiding overwhelm to avoid burdening her parents, and a parent noticing withdrawal and inviting her to state her needs.

"Nandini, dinner's on the table."
"I'm fine, Baba. Not hungry."
"You said that at lunch too."
"I had biscuits. I'm fine. The model's due tomorrow, that's all."
"Is that why your light was on at two last night?"
"...Maybe."
"And the headache you keep rubbing?"
"It's nothing. You're already tired from your shift. I didn't want to add stuff."
Anirban pulled a chair up beside her desk and sat down.
"Nandini, you are not 'stuff'. If you're tired, hungry or stuck, I want to know. That isn't being needy. It's just telling me the weather inside."
"...I'm tired. And hungry. And I can't get the motor bit to work."
"Okay. Plate first, then we look at the motor together. And next time you're this swamped, tell me at lunch, not at midnight."
"Deal. Can the plate have two rotis?"
"Three."

qa.q: When was Nandini's light on last night?
qa.a: Nandini's light was on at two last night.

qa.q: Why did Nandini keep saying 'I'm fine'?
qa.a: Nandini felt overwhelmed and tired, but was worried about being a burden while Baba was already tired from his shift. She may also have felt embarrassed about being stuck.

qa.q: What did Anirban notice, and how did it help?
qa.a: Anirban noticed the skipped meals, the late light and the headache, sat down beside her and said her needs were not 'stuff', which made it safe to say tired, hungry and stuck.

qa.q: If you were Anirban, what would you want after hearing 'I'm fine' again?
qa.a: You'd want the truth early, at lunch rather than at midnight, so a small problem doesn't grow and you can actually help.

grounding: It shows a teenager hiding tiredness, hunger and overwhelm behind 'I'm fine' to avoid burdening a parent, and the parent noticing and inviting plain statements of need.
